text: Six children look over a wall at a beach.
From up here they see all of it at once. They cannot touch any of it.
Then they go down.
On the sand there is no view of the whole. There is a ball, cold water, and whatever happens next. Here they can change things.
Nobody on the sand knows how the day will end.
Later they climb back up. The beach is empty.
The day has not gone. It has gone behind them. Time moves forward, so what is done is at their backs, and they turn round to look at it.
Looking back is looking from outside.
Walk out of your house and you can see its whole shape. You cannot move a chair.
Go back in and you can move the chair. You have lost the shape.
Nobody gets both at once.
A jigsaw puts it on a table. On the lid is the whole picture. In your hand is one piece.
Living is the pieces. Remembering is the lid.
The lid is not a photograph, though. Each time we remember, we make the picture again from a few bright pieces, and it comes out a little different.
Kierkegaard said it in two sentences. Life must be understood backwards. It must be lived forwards.
Now step further back. A day is one piece. So is a year. So is a life.
From inside, a life feels like the next thing to do. From outside it has a shape, and people have always told that shape as a story.
Joseph Campbell called it the hero's journey: leave home, be tested, come back changed. Maureen Murdock answered with the heroine's journey, which is as much a return as a quest.
Ursula Le Guin went further. She said the first tool was probably not a spear. It was a bag: something to carry things home in, and to carry them to someone else.
The small self holds the piece. The large self is the picture. We are both, and we mostly forget the second.
Look again at the wall the children are leaning on. Somebody built it, long before they were born.
Most of what holds us up was made by people we will never meet. We are doing the same, now, for people who will never meet us.
William Blake pictured that work as a city: ever building, ever falling.
To remember is, in a way, to re-member: to put the members back together. Nobody does that alone.
There is a trap in looking back. Suppose you only ever rehearsed the day you have.
You would score better and better on it, and worse on every new day. You would become very good at being who you were yesterday.
A measure that becomes the only target stops measuring. That is Goodhart's law.
Try to remember, not what happened when you were five, but how the world looked. You know it was different. You cannot say how. The ruler itself has changed.
So something has to loosen the join. At night the clock stops mattering. The ball rolls uphill. The sea is in the wrong place. Nobody minds.
Everyone you meet in a dream is made by you. For a few hours you are the whole beach.
The dots are shaken and joined again. What comes out is not yesterday repeated. It is yesterday transformed.
One idea in science is that this is what dreams are for. They stop us fitting too closely to the days we have had. It is a hypothesis. The arithmetic behind it is sound.
In the morning you are somewhere again. Not everywhere, not nowhere, and not quite where you were.
The lid goes back on the shelf. The pieces are on the table, and one of them is in your hand.
That is what the beach is for. Go down again.
